prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and trade exposure reshape labour demand, wage inequality and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: B006 as a single part, credited to Autor, Hanson and Katz. My reasoning is sharper after the exchange. The achievement is a framework for how technology and trade shift labour demand and the wage structure, paired with design-based evidence on where adjustment costs fall. The work is mature, since the skill-premium line is about three decades old, the task framework over two decades and the trade-shock papers over a decade. Replication, extension to other countries and sustained critique have not overturned the core finding. The live debates concern the size and persistence of the effects and shift-share inference, not whether the effects exist. The citation should therefore claim what has been shown, namely effects on labour demand, wage inequality and local adjustment, and should not assert a settled long-run magnitude or origination of the task framework. In answer to the chair's question on what changed my view: I moved from B007 to B006 after Boppart, Strömberg and Teorell argued that identification of constitutional and electoral-rule effects is weaker than the design-based labour evidence. That is a scientific argument I can evaluate without knowing how others ranked. My opening already had B006 second, and I should say plainly that the cleaner B007 credit line was part of why I ranked it first. I now weigh breadth of confirmation and identification above credit cleanliness. I do not rely on the count of colleagues who prefer B006, and I would hold this position if the count were different.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weakest point. The cap cuts through the credit. Dorn is a central co-author of the China-shock papers and goes unrecognised. Levy, Murnane and Acemoglu contributed to the task framework and sit outside the credited set. Katz's best-known education-technology work was done with a recent laureate, so his marginal claim is the most exposed in the trio. Strömberg and Teorell say the same. The 2023 and 2024 prizes are thematically adjacent, and the committee should be able to say what this prize adds. B006 could also be read as two discoveries, technology and trade, joined by a common outcome. B007 has cleaner credit and a distinct formal agenda, and B009 has a clean two-name credit. If the committee concludes that the single-discovery test cannot be met with Katz, the Autor, Dorn, Hanson variant is the principled fallback, and I would accept it. I would not accept a citation that cannot state its distinct contribution relative to the 2023 and 2024 prizes.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B007 and ranks B006 sixth in his opening. He would credit only Autor and Hanson, because he reads B006 as two related lines (tasks and skill demand, and import competition) and does not want Katz's education-technology work set alongside a prize already given in 2023. He names empirical identification as the weak flank of B007 and says his case should survive without his vote and mine.
responses.response: I agree that your case for B007 should be tested without my vote, and I have tried to do that. After the exchange I do not find it stronger than B006 on the common criteria. The two-name Autor-Hanson set is coherent and avoids the Katz-versus-Dorn problem, but it covers only the task and trade-shock evidence and leaves out the skill-demand account that explains why the shocks matter for the wage structure. Your own concession that identification of constitutional effects is the weak flank is the point that moved me. I accept that a two-name prize is a live option if the committee cannot word a single citation across both strands without restating the 2023 prize. I would then prefer Autor, Dorn, Hanson over Autor and Hanson, because Dorn's co-authorship of the China-shock papers is a specific contribution. I would not add Dorn as a fourth name, since the three-person limit holds.

responses.point: Strömberg prefers B006 with Autor, Hanson and Katz, but says Katz's marginal claim is the most exposed part of the trio because his best-known education-technology work was done with a recent laureate. He names Autor, Dorn and Hanson as the natural fallback within the same discovery.
responses.response: I agree that this is the right way to frame the choice, and I would not defend Katz on seniority or by pointing to the three-name limit. My defence is narrower. His wage-structure and skill-premium work is a separate contribution from the education-technology race book, and it supplies the supply-and-demand account into which the task and trade evidence fits. I should say that I have field proximity here, since my own work on capital-skill complementarity addresses the skill premium. That is a reason to hold the claim to a high bar. If the committee judges that his independent contribution is thin once the Goldin-linked work is set aside, I would move to Autor, Dorn, Hanson. I would make that move on the credit judgement and without changing my view of the scientific merit of the discovery.

responses.point: Hassler, who chairs, moved from B032 to B006 in round 1. He accepts a substitution of Dorn for Katz if the committee decides the trade-shock evidence is the core. He argues that the 2024 prize makes the timing for B007 less comfortable, and he treats the collateral-constraint mechanism as strong but narrower, with limited direct empirical testing.
responses.response: I agree with your treatment of B032. The mechanism is foundational and its attribution to Kiyotaki and Moore is clean, but confirmation is largely indirect, and that matters when set against B006's replication record. On B007 I hold a slightly different view. I do not think the 2024 prize duplicates the formal political-economics agenda, and I said so in round 1. My reason for placing it second is therefore identification and my own disclosed tie, not timing. I would add one thing to your point about the Dorn substitution. The committee should decide it on the specific question of what the citation covers, and should do so before the vote. It should not leave the choice to whichever configuration has more support.

responses.point: Teorell prefers B006 and calls Katz's overlap with the Goldin-linked work the committee's closest call within B006. He also says that if the committee wants a single separable mechanism, B004 or B007 may offer a cleaner story, though B004 has more severe attribution problems.
responses.response: I agree that B004 has the more severe attribution problem. Andersson's case on influence and maturity is strong, and I do not dispute it. But a trio of Taylor, Woodford and Calvo would leave out the estimated and empirical strand, and Andersson has said himself that this is a real judgement. I did not rank B004 above B006 for that reason. On B007 you note its adjacency to your own field. I have the corresponding issue, since Persson is at my home institute, so the case for B007 would need to stand on arguments from members without that proximity. On Katz I share your view that this is the closest call. My answer to the chair's question is that a citation worded around labour demand, wage structure and adjustment to trade and technology can include his wage-structure contribution without restating the 2023 prize. If drafting shows it cannot, I would move to the Dorn variant.

uncertainties: Whether Katz or Dorn is the better third name. The outcome depends on whether the committee can word one citation that covers the skill-premium strand without restating the 2023 prize.
Whether the committee treats technology and trade as one discovery or two. If two, the single-part configuration may need either a narrower citation or a different configuration.
How far the persistence debate and shift-share inference concerns should weigh on the maturity judgement, as opposed to the wording of the citation.
How the committee should credit contributors to the task framework who sit outside the credited set (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu).
Whether B007 would deserve a higher place if the identification concerns prove narrower than colleagues suggest. My own tie to Persson means I cannot judge that on my own.
statement.conflict_note: Persson, a credited name on B007, is at IIES, my home institute. B007 is my first listed alternative, and I disclose this without adjudicating it. I have co-authored with Timo Boppart (co-opted member), and I am a long-term co-author of John Hassler (chair), and both ranked B006 first in round 1. My own work on capital-skill complementarity is close to the skill-premium strand of B006. No tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn is apparent from my supplied profile. I have tried to apply the same criteria used for the other candidates.
